How is knowledge transferred, stored and recalled across generations, and how can the preservation of tradition-based knowledge be most effectively used to deliver innovative outcomes for family firms across industries, time and contexts?

Collectively, the studies examined note that certain factors yield a distinct advantage, and some simultaneously impose a liability, to family-firm KM. For instance, the commonly examined resource of family social capital is noted to exert conflicting effects on certain KM processes. Whether family social capital yields a positive or negative effect depends, in part, on the family members engaged and the nature of their relationships. Although family social capital and related family dynamics are commonly researched in family firms, we are yet to fully understand what, when and how individual-level factors drive group and firmlevel behaviors.

Following the call of De Massis and Foss (2018), the use of a microfoundational perspective is likely to yield valuable insights by fostering investigation into the interrelated effects of the emotions, memories and experiences of family (and nonfamily) members in the family firm.

Relational bondseven those steeped in trust and developed over timeare not impenetrable. As noted by Humphrey et al. (2021), exploring the psychological foundations of (knowledge) management in family firms will offer clarity into how and why strategic behaviors differ from nonfamily firms and highlight differences among family firms. To support this pursuit, the integration of theories and insights from psychology are needed to better understand the relationships among emotions, memories and experiences and to gain insight into how these elements affect collective dynamics that result in firm-level processes such as KM:

RQ2. What theories and insights from psychology (and related disciplines) can be applied to advance our understanding of family-firm KM antecedents, processes, outcomes and moderators, and how do individual-level cognition, emotions and experiences affect group/family dynamics and family-firm behaviors?
6.2 Antecedents: insights and opportunities

An overview of the antecedents studied highlights the importance of trust-based relationships to family firms and their KM processes. For each KM process, nearly all antecedents either directly (or indirectly) relate to trust. For example, family social capital is founded in a deep level of trust that develops over a long period of time among family members. When this level of trust exists, the family firm is able to enhance its knowledge creation, knowledge transfer and knowledge application. However, there is a downside: the trust that resides within family social capital also creates an insularity among kin, limiting the firm's knowledge creation and knowledge transfer. Family social capital is shown to be imperfectly imitable by nonfamily members (Herrero, 2018) and exists in at least three broad configurations (Sanchez-Ruiz et al., 2019). While these and other studies advance our understanding of family social capital, how can family firms achieve optimal value creation wherein the benefits of family social capital are maximized and the negative effects minimized?
RQ3. How can family social capital be optimally leveraged by the family firm to deliver maximum value creation for each type of knowledge process?

Each antecedent also relates, in some form, to the family. The family is a source of difference among family firms. The dynamics of the family are regularly noted as influential to KM processes. For example, Zahra (2012) notes the importance of family cohesion, with more cohesive families having enhanced capabilities with respect to some KM processes, offering evidence that internal family dynamics matter. Given this importance, a refined understanding of the family will allow for a more robust understanding of the family firm. Jaskiewicz and Dyer (2017) note the following four common dimensions of families that are derived from family science theories: family structures, family functions, family interactions and family events. Along this line, to better understand KM processes and related differences among family firms, more remains to be known about the differences among families. Jaskiewicz and Dyer (2017) note numerous opportunities for integrating family science theories [12] into management, and accordingly, we look forward to a better understanding of the differences among families given that such insights will have valuable implications for understanding what, how, when and why family firms strategically develop and leverage KM processes:
RQ4. How do differences in and among families, as well as varied definitions of "family," affect family-firm KM processes?

Family firms tend to pursue a broader set of outcomes than nonfamily firms (Holt et al., 2017). Developing and maintaining SEW is a salient noneconomic goal for many (perhaps all) family firms (Berrone et al., 2012). However, the scope of noneconomic goals is expansive for families and their firms, and investigating the effects of these goals on KM processes presents numerous opportunities. Particularly, future researchers can consider the effects of the family's desire to maintain control over the firm and the extent to which (and how) this desire affects KM processes. Maintaining control allows the family firm to prioritize desired goals; however, questions related to which noneconomic goals enhance (and which restrict) the development of KM processes remain to be answered. Following the work of Miller and Le Breton-Miller (2014), extended SEW goals may support the superior growth and development of KM processes, yet do restricted SEW goals, which are focused on more immediate outcomes for the family, always hinder KM processes? If not, in what conditions might the family's short-term, family-centered, noneconomic goals enhance the KM processes of the family firm? Studies suggest that conflicts may arise among family and business priorities, giving rise to a potential "dark side" of family influence (Biscotti et al., 2018). Although studies have begun to examine the effects of family-centered, noneconomic goals, more work is needed to determine what, how and when KM processes enable a family firm to achieve these desired outcomes. Moreover, expanding the scope of outcomes examinedto include a broader range of nonfinancial outcomeswill offer greater clarity on the types of outcomes pursued and the extent to which they are achieved:

RQ5. What noneconomic goals affect KM processes, how do KM processes allow family firms to achieve noneconomic outcomes, and how does the potential conflict between financial and nonfinancial pursuits affect investments in family-firm KM?

div.head: Outcomes: insights and opportunities
div.p: Reviewing family-firm KM studies also presents insights and opportunities for future research related to the outcomes of KM processes. Prior research highlights the importance of protecting and preserving the family's identity (Magistretti et al., 2020). Some family firms use branding strategies to communicate the family and corporate heritage via their company website as a strategy to preserve their family identity (Micelotta and Raynard, 2011). Future research is needed to examine what other approaches are successfully used by family firms (and families) to preserve their heritage and imprint an entrepreneurial legacy (Jaskiewicz et al., 2015).

Family firms may seek to preserve the beliefs and knowledge that constitute their traditions, yet, at the same time, family firms must innovate to remain competitive. Extending the work of De Massis et al. (2016), which examines family firms that innovate through tradition, Erdogan et al. (2020) note that innovation and tradition create a paradox. They note that family firms can successfully navigate the paradox through a specific capability. Building on these insights, how can family firms remain competitive while preserving their organizational memory and traditions? It is noted that the storage and recall of knowledge is essential, yet much remains to be understood about the processes through which longer-surviving family firms are able to effectively store, recall, reinterpret and apply knowledge to innovate through tradition. Understanding these knowledge processes holds noteworthy promise:
RQ6. What is the process through which family firms are able to engage in activities like "innovating through tradition" to enhance transgenerational survival and success?

In this review, some antecedents are observed to offer both positive and negative effects on KM processes (e.g. family social capital, SEW preservation intentions). Additionally, KM processes are noted to have varied effects on outcomes. However, more comprehensive studies are needed to examine the longitudinal and multi-level effects that antecedents have on KM processes, which thereby yield categorically different and varied levels of outcomes.

Furthermore, work that examines multiple KM processes simultaneously is particularly interesting. A recent study by Mun ˜oz-Bull on et al. (2020) empirically demonstrates that family firms using a combined innovation strategywherein innovation activities occur both in the firm and are outsourced to third partiesachieve greater innovation outcomes compared to nonfamily firms with similar strategies. The family firm's ability to gain this type of competitive advantage is attributed to being selective and establishing trust-based relationships with external partners (Duran et al., 2016), their organizational and family social capital (Arregle et al., 2007;Sanchez-Ruiz et al., 2019), noneconomic goals such as reputation (Berrone et al., 2012) and related factors. Insights like these, which take a more holistic approach to understanding the (paradoxical) effects on KM processes, the simultaneous use of multiple KM processes, and the outcomes obtained as a result are likely to offer notable advances to family-firm KM scholarship:

RQ7. What and how do multi-level factors affect family-firm KM processes, how are paradoxical challenges related to KM overcome by family firms and used to create a competitive advantage, and what (non)economic outcomes are generated over time?

div.head: Moderators: insights and opportunities
div.p: The relationships among antecedents, KM processes and outcomes vary given relevant boundary conditions. Our review identifies moderating effects that are commonly examined across studies, and among these, the extent of the family's involvement is commonly observed. Even though the involvement of the family leads to potentially valuable and unique resources and capabilities, the family firm composed only of kin may, at some point, need to hire nonfamily members to grow and/or acquire the resources needed to survive (Stewart and Hitt, 2012). In family firms with heightened family social capital, the involvement of nonfamily members is noted to enhance the ability of the firm to acquire and transfer external knowledge; however, nonfamily members also mitigate the benefits of family social capital for knowledge application purposes. Given that hiring nonfamily members is likely to be required for many family firms, and because the vast majority of family firms employ nonfamily members (Tabor et al., 2018), how can jobs for nonfamily (and family) be designed so that maximum value is created for and from the family firm's KM processes?

RQ8. Leveraging insights from human resource management, what is the optimal job design for the relevant positions in the family firm that yields the greatest benefit to KM processes and provides the maximum attainment of desired outcomes?

div.head: Additional insights and opportunities
div.p: Knowledge is typically created through collaborative mechanisms (Nonaka, 1994). In comparison to nonfamily firms, family firms often provide family members with opportunities for social interactions. Of the studies reviewed, several compare family and nonfamily firms with respect to the antecedents and outcomes of their KM processes. For instance, Debicki et al. (2020) investigate the strategic approaches of family and nonfamily firms and the effects on relational capital, finding that unique family resources enhance the firm's knowledge application.

There is a substantially greater contingent of studies, however, that examines family firm heterogeneity [13]. The differences among family firms have been examined by exploring different levels of family ownership (Kotlar et al., 2020;Sciascia and Mazzola, 2008;Zahra, 2012), family involvement in the TMT (Pittino et al., 2018), generational involvement (Chirico et al., 2011) and nonfamily member involvement (Randolph et al., 2021), etc. Although the majority of studies examined investigate differences among family firms, much remains to be understood about family-firm heterogeneity. Daspit et al. (2021: 3) define family-firm heterogeneity as "the range of categorical and/or variational difference(s) between or among family firms at a given time or across time." Based on this definition, what are the various facets of difference that exist among family firms with respect to KM processes? Additionally, how do these differences evolve over time?
RQ9. What are the categorical, variational, spatial and temporal differences among family firms with respect to their KM antecedents, processes and outcomes?

Finally, studies related to KM in general (not specific to family firms) have appeared in an array of journals, crossing disciplinary boundaries. Given this scope, numerous theoretical perspectives have been used to examine KM. Specifically, Matayong and Mahmood (2013) reviewed KM literature and identified these nine theories that are the most common theoretical frameworks of general KM studies: innovation diffusion theory, the theory of reasoned action, the technology acceptance model, the theory of planned behavior, tasktechnology fit, social capital theory, social cognitive theory, the IS success model and the IS continuance model. For the study of KM to move forward, Paoloni et al. (2020) note that KM research will benefit from recognizing and more closely examining the role of social capital and related factors.

Looking forward, KM researchers may benefit by integrating insights from family-firm scholarship given the unique relational dynamics that manifest in this context. With the coupling of the family and business systems, unique (social) resources and capabilities are created (Habbershon and Williams, 1999;Habbershon et al., 2003). In their seminal work, Pearson et al. (2008) take a social capital perspective of familiness and elucidate the unique structural, cognitive and relational resources, as well as the unique capabilities (i.e. refined knowledge and associability capabilities) that create idiosyncratic value for the family firm. However, while the social capital created among family is "imperfectly imitable" by nonfamily firms (Herrero, 2018), not all family firms have similar levels of family social capital (Sanchez-Ruiz et al., 2019). Therefore, given that family firms are the most common form of business, KM researchers are encouraged to consider the extent of family involvement in the organizations studied and account for family-specific influences, like family social capital, to obtain more precise insights.

Further, Durst and Edvardsson (2012) note in their review of KM that more work is needed to address both the sender and the receiver involved in the knowledge-transfer process (many studies focus on one side). Here too, the study of family firms can be potentially helpful given that family-firm scholars use an array of perspectives to understand the involvement of nonfamily members in the family firm. For instance, agency, stewardship, social capital, expectancy, commitment, psychological ownership and other perspectives have been employed to examine nonfamily members (see review by Tabor et al., 2018). These, and other, perspectives can be used to better understand both sides of the knowledge-transfer process and more accurately account for differences between the actors engaged in the exchange:

RQ10. What perspectives and insights can be leveraged from family-firm scholarship to advance the study of KM more broadly, and what perspectives from KM can be leveraged to advance family-firm scholarship?

div.head: Limitations
div.p: Although this review contributes to both family-business and KM scholarship, the contributions are not without limitations. First, we examine family-firm KM literature by categorizing the articles based on four KM processes including knowledge creation, storage/retrieval, transfer and application. While this conceptualization is consistent with the seminal work of Alavi and Leidner (2001), we recognize that other conceptualizations of KM processes exist and are relevant. Nonetheless, by basing the review on a well-accepted conceptualization, we organize insights in a manner that can be broadly understood. Second, in the review, we identify key antecedents, outcomes and moderators; however, we elected to not review the relationships between and among KM processes. Although some studies examine such relationships, we forego such detail for the purpose of parsimony. Nonetheless, when an identified study examined more than one KM process, each process was coded, and when possible, we focused the review on the primary aspect of KM examined. Third, while we review an array of factors, the intention is not to reference every construct and relationship identified in the literature. Instead, we note key factors and represent the general nature of the relationship(s) observed while fully acknowledging that differences in context and magnitude create differing effects. Fourth, given the expansive nature of the review, we purposefully reserve methodological observations. Method-related advances are, indeed, necessary to the advancement of knowledge on family-firm KM processes, and we look forward to work that offers promising ways to enhance the empirical study of family-firm KM processes.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this review, we aim to reduce the fragmentation in the family-firm KM literature. Based on insights from 74 articles published in 23 journals, we coalesce findings into a framework that highlights antecedents, outcomes and moderators related to KM processes in the family firm. Additionally, we offer a summary of integrated insights and identify promising opportunities for future research with the intention of helping to advance scholarly work in the fields of family business and KM, both respectively and in a complementary manner. While much work remains to be done, we look forward to future insights that will advance our understanding of KM in family firms.
